sections.markdown:
## C — Reading the road, the following-distance count, the space cushion and tailgaters, blind spots, entering and crossing traffic, communicating with signals, and passing on the left and right
Knowledge domain: how far ahead and around to look, how to measure and keep a safe gap from the vehicle ahead, how to handle tailgaters and blind spots, how to enter traffic, when and how far ahead to signal, and the steps and limits for passing.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Keep your eyes moving and read the road about one city block ahead, so you are not forced into last-minute decisions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
As you approach an intersection, look both left and right before you continue. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
Checking the rearview mirror often shows you where traffic behind you is and warns you when someone is tailgating or closing in too fast. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
When you keep track of how fast and where the traffic is in front, behind and on both sides, you can make decisions quickly and safely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
The manual's 3-6 second rule tests your gap: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point such as a sign or overpass, start counting, and if you reach that point before you finish, you are following too closely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
Counting from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four takes about four seconds. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
The faster you go, the greater your following distance should be. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A01
Poor road conditions call for more than a 3-second cushion, so give yourself 3 to 6 seconds. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A01
Space around your vehicle gives you and other drivers time to react to emergencies, and staying in the middle of your lane helps create that cushion. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A01
Keep enough room ahead of you to stop suddenly, and enough room ahead and behind to pass or stop safely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A01
At high speed you travel farther while reacting to a problem, so your margin for error shrinks. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A01
Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A01
When you share a lane with a bicycle, keep at least 3 feet between your vehicle and the rider and moderate your speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A01
You help the driver behind you keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A01
If someone is tailgating you, slow down gradually and open more space ahead, so you can brake more gently and give the tailgater time to react [A01] [A02].
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A02
When it is safe, changing to another lane encourages a tailgater to go around you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A02
What you do affects the driver behind you, especially when you have to stop suddenly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A02
Blind spots are the areas at the left and right sides of your vehicle that your mirrors do not show. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A02
When cars parked near an intersection or bushes, trees or buildings block your view, creep forward slowly until you can see clearly, then go when the way is clear. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A02
Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, watching for motorcycles too, by speeding up or dropping back rather than lingering beside them. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A02
Make sure other drivers can see your vehicle, and do not trust your mirrors alone to show vehicles or motorcycles beside you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A02
Look over your shoulder to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A02
When entering the road from a side road or a private drive, stop and wait until traffic clears. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A02
Do not assume a vehicle or motorcycle with its turn signal on will really turn; wait until you see the driver commit to the turn before you pull out. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A02
Use your turn signals whenever you change direction, such as moving to another lane, turning at an intersection, merging onto a freeway, leaving a curb or pulling off the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A02
Signal out of habit even when no one else seems to be around, because the vehicle or motorcycle you have not noticed poses the greatest danger. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A02
Communicating means showing other drivers and pedestrians what you intend to do early enough to prevent a collision. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A02
Signal at least 100 feet, roughly 4 seconds, before you turn so others have time to react. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A02
If your turn comes just past an intersection, wait until you are inside the intersection to signal, because drivers there could pull into your path. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A02
After you finish your move, make sure the turn signal has gone off. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A03
A signal warns others of your move and gives them time to react, but it does not give you the right-of-way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A03
You may show a turn with your turn signals, with hand signals, or with both. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A03
The law sets the lanes and positions you must use for turns and requires a signal at least 100 feet before you turn. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A03
Always signal before changing lanes, turning at an intersection or into a driveway or alley, entering or leaving a freeway, pulling away from the curb, or pulling over to the side of the road. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A03
When you are using hand signals, also signal before you slow down or stop suddenly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A03
To pass a vehicle or motorcycle going your way, signal the lane change and pass on the left. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A03
Before passing, be sure you have the time and room to get completely ahead of the other vehicle without endangering oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A03
Return to the right lane once you can see the whole front, or both headlights, of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror, after a shoulder check and a signal. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A03
The same passing steps apply when you pass slow-moving motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F41 | anchor: A03
If a vehicle behind you honks or flashes its lights to pass, move right when it is safe and let it by, and never speed up while you are being passed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F42 | anchor: A03
Passing on the right is permitted only when safe and either the driver ahead is turning left, you are on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes in your direction, or you are in a business or residential district marked for two or more lanes in your direction; never leave the paved or main roadway to pass on the right, and never pass to the left of a driver signaling a left turn [A03] [FXS0028].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec06-F43 | anchor: A03
Passing on the right is also allowed on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes moving in your direction. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0027]

Misconceptions: a turn signal from the other driver is not proof they will turn, so wait for the turn to begin; signaling never hands you the right-of-way; the mirrors alone do not clear a lane change, a shoulder check does; when you are being passed, the safe response is to let the other vehicle by, never to race it.
Mnemonics: Count it out to the fixed point — finish the count before you get there; pass left, return when both headlights show in the mirror.
Glossary: space cushion means the open space kept around your vehicle on every side; blind spot means a side area your mirrors cannot show; tailgating means following another vehicle too closely; committing to a turn means visibly beginning the turn rather than only signaling it.
Dynamic facts: the rules in this section are stable driving technique and statute; the third condition for passing on the right continues on the following page and is taught with that page.
